title: Historical Entity
description: A node in the hierarchical history tree. Regions, Eras, Periods, Reigns, Events, Taxa and Thresholds all share this shape. Parent/child links form the tree. Schema 3.1.0 adds the `received` dating method for dates handed down by tradition rather than measured or attested. Schema 3.0.0 replaces the single `dating_method` with per-boundary `start_dating_method` / `end_dating_method`, resolving Q-30; consumers reading `dating_method` at entity level will find nothing, hence the MAJOR bump. Within `alternatives`, `dating_method` is retained and correct, because an alternative is a claim about a single boundary. Schema 2.0.0 added the 'taxon' and 'threshold' kinds and the 'minimum' date precision, and restructured prehistory ids. Schema 1.1.0 added subkind, dating_method, standing, as_of, native_date, alternatives, caveats and source_ids.

id.description: Stable, human-readable slug. Use dot-notation to reflect hierarchy, e.g. 'africa.nile.egypt.new-kingdom.dyn-19.ramesses-ii'. Segment-strict pattern: lowercase alnum segments joined by '.' or '-'.

kind.description: region = geographic bucket; era = long civilizational chunk; period = dynasty/named sub-era/nengō; reign = single ruler; event = discrete moment (battle, treaty, disaster); taxon = a biological species or population (a taxon is NOT a period — several outlive the eras they are filed near, and Homo sapiens is extant); threshold = the earliest known instance of a behaviour, e.g. controlled fire. A threshold is a ONE-SIDED bound: new evidence can only move it older, and the behaviour continues after it. Use date_precision 'minimum' with it.

name.description: Primary display name in the UI's default language.

native_name.description: Endonym / original-script name where applicable (e.g. '明治', 'Tawantinsuyu').

aliases.description: Flat list of alternate names, used for search matching. DERIVED from name_forms at build time when name_forms is present -- do not hand-author both, or they drift. Hand-authored aliases remain valid for entities with no naming complexity.

name_forms.description: Structured alternate names. A flat string list cannot say why a name differs, who uses it, when it applied, or whether anyone repudiates it -- which is why the hard cases went unfilled while King Tut and Cheops got aliases. Each form carries its own kind so search can index all of them while the UI groups them meaningfully.

kind.description: endonym: what it called itself. exonym: an outsiders' name. formal: official long form. common: everyday short form. translation: the same referent in another language. scholarly: a modern academic coinage with no ancient referent. historical: used only during a stated period. rejected: actively repudiated by descendant communities.

lang.description: BCP-47 tag. The display name is implicitly the English form; this makes that assumption visible rather than silent.

from.description: First year this form was in use, when the form is period-bound.

to.description: Last year this form was in use.

note.description: One sentence on where the form comes from or why it is rejected.

source_ids.description: Ids into the normalized source registry. Deduplicated rather than inlined: one chronology work cited by 200 entities is stored once.

parent_id.description: id of the parent entity; explicitly null for top-level regions. Must always be present.

cross_parent_ids.description: Additional non-primary parents for cross-region entities (e.g. Mongol Empire is Steppe primary, but also cross-parents into East Asia and West Asia).

regions.description: DERIVED, not authored: the top-level geographies this entity is reachable from, following parent_id and cross_parent_ids in both directions. Present only when more than one. This records where an entity is PLACED, not where a polity RULED -- the Mongol empire understates at two regions because its khanates are ordinary children whose own cross-links do not propagate upward. A territorial claim would have to be authored with sources.

start_year.description: Start year (proleptic Gregorian, no year zero). Negative = BCE. null = unknown or not-applicable. Always present.

end_year.description: End year (proleptic Gregorian). Negative = BCE. null = ongoing/present or unknown. Always present.

start_year_min.description: Earliest plausible start year across scholarly disagreement. Defaults to start_year.

start_year_max.description: Latest plausible start year across scholarly disagreement. Defaults to start_year.

end_year_min.description: Earliest plausible end year. Defaults to end_year.

end_year_max.description: Latest plausible end year. Defaults to end_year.

date_precision.description: Overall precision when a single value fits both endpoints. If start and end have different precisions, use start_precision / end_precision instead. 'exact' is retained as an alias for 'year'. 'minimum' means the date is a floor, not an estimate: the behaviour or occurrence is at least this old and may be older. It is the correct precision for a threshold, where the record can only be pushed back.

date_note.description: Free-text note about dating (source disagreement, traditional-vs-attested, calendar transitions, etc.).

allow_outside_parent_dates.description: Set true when this entity's dates legitimately fall outside its parent's dates (co-ruler tenure, span-crossing figure, historiographic bucket). Silences the containment warning.

summary.description: One or two sentences suitable for a tooltip or side-panel. Written for a general reader.

tier.description: Novice-friendliness tier for progressive disclosure. 'foundational' = well-known to general audiences; 'specialist' = deep cuts. Always present.

calendar_ids.description: Calendar systems most-associated with this entity (Japanese nengō for Japan, Hijri for Islamic states, etc.).

notable_figures.description: Free-text notable people not modeled as separate reign entities.

capital.description: Capital city (if applicable, and if a single value suffices).

links.description: Typed relations to other entities beyond simple parent/successor links. Use when the semantic type matters (successor_state_of, conquered_by, co_ruler_with, etc.).

type.description: The semantic relation. `rival_claimant_to` is for two entities claiming the SAME sovereignty or office at the same time, which is different from ordinary overlap: Champa and Vietnam coexisted as neighbours, but the Fatimids and Abbasids both claimed the caliphate. Simple coexistence needs no link at all — most of history overlaps.

start_dating_method.description: How the START boundary's date was arrived at. Orthogonal to precision: a calibrated radiocarbon date and an attested king-list date can share a precision while being entirely different kinds of claim. Selects whether the readout leads in BP or in calendar reckoning, which is computed from the start. Schema 3.0.0 split the former single `dating_method` into per-boundary fields (Q-30): one field cannot describe an entity whose boundaries rest on different science. Schema 3.1.0 adds `received`, for a date arrived at by transmission rather than by measurement or attestation: Rome's 753 BCE from the annalists, Narmer's 3100 from king-lists, the Namazga phase brackets from Masson's ceramic typology. Before it, such entities carried no method at all, because calling them `typological` or `unknown` misdescribed a date whose provenance is in fact perfectly well known — it is just not evidence. Schema 3.3.0 adds `dendrochronology`. Its absence was conspicuous: the American Southwest is where Douglass invented tree-ring dating, and filing Chaco under radiocarbon made the readout offer 'cal BP' for sites dated to the year.

end_dating_method.description: How the END boundary's date was arrived at, when it differs from the start. Neanderthals appear at ~400 ka by uranium-series and disappear at ~40 ka by radiocarbon; recording one method for both is the error this field exists to prevent. Omit when the end is undated or the method is unrecorded -- it is NOT inherited from the start, because silently inheriting is what produced the mislabelling. Schema 3.1.0 adds `received`, for a date arrived at by transmission rather than by measurement or attestation: Rome's 753 BCE from the annalists, Narmer's 3100 from king-lists, the Namazga phase brackets from Masson's ceramic typology. Before it, such entities carried no method at all, because calling them `typological` or `unknown` misdescribed a date whose provenance is in fact perfectly well known — it is just not evidence.

standing.description: How the date stands relative to the field. `traditional` is deliberately separate: received dates such as Rome's 753 BCE founding are not findings, and presenting them with the same weight as measured or attested dates is the commonest way a history reference misleads.

as_of.description: ISO date this dating was last checked against the literature. Only for genuinely open disputes: a date-stamped controversy is useful, an undated one is a trap because a reader cannot tell whether it was settled last week.

alternatives.description: Rival dating claims. NOT imprecision: three competing chronologies flattened into one wide range implies the middle is likeliest, when the actual claim is that the field disagrees about which is right.

standing.description: How the date stands relative to the field. `traditional` is deliberately separate: received dates such as Rome's 753 BCE founding are not findings, and presenting them with the same weight as measured or attested dates is the commonest way a history reference misleads.

dating_method.description: How the date was arrived at. Orthogonal to `date_precision`, which is about resolution: a calibrated radiocarbon date and an attested king-list date can share a precision while being entirely different kinds of claim. Also selects whether the readout leads in BP or in calendar reckoning. Schema 3.1.0 adds `received`, for a date arrived at by transmission rather than by measurement or attestation: Rome's 753 BCE from the annalists, Narmer's 3100 from king-lists, the Namazga phase brackets from Masson's ceramic typology. Before it, such entities carried no method at all, because calling them `typological` or `unknown` misdescribed a date whose provenance is in fact perfectly well known — it is just not evidence.

caveats.description: Corrections belonging to the subject rather than to a date. The Ghana Empire was not in modern Ghana; the Maya never formed one empire. Neither is chronological, so neither belongs on a boundary.

text.description: One sentence. Brevity is enforced: prose is where 'starting point, not research tool' quietly erodes.

source_ids.description: Ids into the normalized source registry. Deduplicated rather than inlined: one chronology work cited by 200 entities is stored once.
